text: What is object-oriented programming, and what problems does it solve compared to procedural code?
expectedAnswerPoints: A paradigm built around objects that bundle data (attributes) with the code (methods) that operates on it
Models software using real-world entities such as Car, Student or Account with properties and behaviours
Procedural code lacks modular structure; classes group related data and logic together
Procedural code reuses poorly; inheritance allows existing code to be extended rather than duplicated
Procedural code exposes data freely; encapsulation hides internal state behind controlled access
Overall benefits are modularity, reusability, maintainability and scalability

text: What is the difference between a class and an object?
expectedAnswerPoints: A class is a blueprint or template defining structure and behaviour
An object is a concrete instance of that class, created in memory
A class defines attributes and methods but occupies no memory for instance data until an object exists
Many objects can be created from one class, each with its own attribute values
Analogy: the class is the architectural plan, the object is the actual house built from it

text: Explain the four pillars of OOP.
expectedAnswerPoints: Encapsulation: wrapping data and the methods that act on it into a single unit and restricting direct access to internal state
Inheritance: a derived class acquires properties and behaviour from a base class, promoting code reuse
Polymorphism: the same interface behaves differently depending on context, via overloading or overriding
Abstraction: hiding unnecessary implementation detail and exposing only the essential features
Encapsulation is about hiding data; abstraction is about hiding complexity

text: What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?
expectedAnswerPoints: Encapsulation bundles data with its methods and restricts direct access, typically using private fields with getters and setters
Abstraction hides implementation complexity and exposes only what the caller needs to know
Encapsulation is about how data is protected; abstraction is about what is exposed at the design level
Encapsulation is achieved with access modifiers; abstraction with abstract classes, pure virtual functions or interfaces
Encapsulation is an implementation technique, abstraction is a design principle, and they are usually applied together

text: Explain the private, protected and public access specifiers.
expectedAnswerPoints: Private members are accessible only inside the class that declares them
Protected members are accessible inside the class and in its derived classes
Public members are accessible from anywhere
In Java there is also a default (package-private) level, accessible only within the same package
Private members are not directly accessible in a derived class but still exist in the object and can be reached through inherited public or protected methods

text: What is a constructor? Explain the different types of constructor.
expectedAnswerPoints: A special method invoked automatically when an object is created, used to initialise it
It has the same name as the class and no return type
Default/non-parameterised constructor takes no arguments and is used when no values are supplied
Parameterised constructor accepts arguments to initialise the object at creation time
Copy constructor creates a new object as a copy of an existing one
Memory is allocated before the constructor runs; the constructor only initialises

text: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy?
expectedAnswerPoints: A shallow copy copies the reference or address of dynamically allocated members, so both objects point to the same memory
With a shallow copy, modifying data through one object is visible through the other
A deep copy allocates new memory and copies the actual values, making the objects fully independent
Deep copy is needed when a class owns pointers or dynamically allocated resources
A shallow copy of an object holding a pointer can also cause a double-free or dangling pointer when both destructors run

text: What is a destructor, and why does Java not have one?
expectedAnswerPoints: A destructor is a special member function called automatically when an object goes out of scope or is explicitly deleted
In C++ it shares the class name prefixed with a tilde, takes no parameters and has no return type
It is used to release resources such as heap memory, file handles and connections
Java has no destructors because it uses automatic garbage collection to reclaim unreachable objects
The garbage collector prevents memory leaks without manual deletion, though collection timing is not deterministic
finalize() existed as a rough equivalent but is deprecated due to unpredictability

text: Explain the different types of inheritance.
expectedAnswerPoints: Single: one derived class inherits from one base class
Multilevel: a class derives from a class that is itself derived, forming a chain
Hierarchical: several derived classes inherit from a single base class
Multiple: one class inherits from two or more base classes, supported in C++ but not by classes in Java
Hybrid: a combination of two or more of the above
Java achieves multiple inheritance safely through interfaces rather than classes

text: What is the diamond problem, and how do C++ and Java each deal with it?
expectedAnswerPoints: It occurs in multiple inheritance when classes B and C both inherit from A, and D inherits from both B and C
D then has two copies of A's members, so the compiler cannot tell which one to use, creating ambiguity
In C++ it can be resolved manually with explicit scope resolution, such as obj.B::show()
The proper C++ fix is virtual inheritance, which ensures only one shared copy of the base class exists
Java avoids it by not allowing multiple inheritance of classes
Java uses interfaces for multiple inheritance, and the implementing class must supply its own method definition

text: What is the difference between compile-time and run-time polymorphism?
expectedAnswerPoints: Compile-time (static binding, early binding) resolves the method at compile time based on the signature
Compile-time polymorphism is achieved through method overloading and, in C++, operator overloading
Run-time (dynamic binding, late binding) resolves the method at execution time based on the actual object type
Run-time polymorphism is achieved through method overriding, using virtual functions in C++
Run-time polymorphism lets a base class pointer or reference invoke the derived class implementation

text: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
expectedAnswerPoints: Overloading uses the same method name with different parameter lists within the same class
Overriding redefines a base class method in a derived class with the same name, parameters and return type
Overloading is compile-time polymorphism; overriding is run-time polymorphism
Overloading needs no inheritance; overriding requires an inheritance relationship
Return type alone cannot distinguish overloaded methods
An overriding method must keep the same signature, though Java permits a covariant return type

text: What is a virtual function, and what happens if you omit the virtual keyword in C++?
expectedAnswerPoints: A member function in a base class expected to be overridden in derived classes
Declaring it virtual tells the compiler to use run-time binding instead of compile-time binding
Without virtual, C++ binds based on the pointer or reference type rather than the actual object type
So calling through a base class pointer would run the base class version rather than the derived override
A base class with virtual functions should also have a virtual destructor, otherwise deleting a derived object through a base pointer only runs the base destructor and leaks resources

text: What is an abstract class and a pure virtual function? Why would you use one?
expectedAnswerPoints: An abstract class cannot be instantiated and serves as a base interface for derived classes
In C++ a class becomes abstract by having at least one pure virtual function, declared with = 0
A pure virtual function has no definition in the base class and must be overridden by derived classes
It is used when a generic base concept makes no sense on its own, such as Shape versus Circle or Rectangle
It forces derived classes to provide their own implementation, guaranteeing a consistent interface
An abstract class may still contain concrete methods and data shared by all subclasses

text: In Java, when would you use an abstract class rather than an interface?
expectedAnswerPoints: Use an abstract class when subclasses need to share common implementation or state
Abstract classes can have constructors, instance fields and any access modifier; interfaces cannot have constructors or instance state
Interface fields are implicitly public static final constants
A class can extend only one abstract class but implement many interfaces
Use an interface to declare a capability or contract that unrelated classes can implement
Interfaces can now provide default and static methods, but still cannot hold instance state
